body_text:
The Fundamental Subspace Duality Theorem. For any linear map $T : V \to W$
between finite-dimensional vector spaces:
$$ \ker(T^*) = (\operatorname{im} T)^\circ \quad \text{and} \quad \operatorname{im}(T^*) = (\ker T)^\circ. $$

*Proof*:
1. A functional $\psi \in W^*$ satisfies $\psi \in \ker(T^*)$ if and only if
   $T^*(\psi) = \psi \circ T = 0$. This means $\psi(T(v)) = 0$ for all $v \in V$,
   which by definition states that $\psi$ annihilates $\operatorname{im}(T)$.
   Thus $\ker(T^*) = (\operatorname{im} T)^\circ$.
2. Applying dimensions: $\dim(\operatorname{im} T^*) = \dim(W^*) - \dim(\ker T^*) = \dim(W) - \dim((\operatorname{im} T)^\circ) = \dim(\operatorname{im} T)$.
   Hence $\operatorname{rank}(T^*) = \operatorname{rank}(T)$ (row rank equals column rank).
   Since $T^*(\psi)(\ker T) = \psi(T(\ker T)) = \psi(0) = 0$, we have
   $\operatorname{im}(T^*) \subseteq (\ker T)^\circ$.
   Since both subspaces have dimension $\dim(V) - \dim(\ker T) = \operatorname{rank}(T)$,
   they are equal: $\operatorname{im}(T^*) = (\ker T)^\circ$.
   
This theorem forms the structural core of the Fredholm Alternative for linear
systems: $Ax = b$ has a solution if and only if $b$ is annihilated by every
solution $y$ to the homogeneous dual system $y^T A = 0$.
